newsitem.title: UK: Buba seen unwilling to use rates as mark booster.
newsitem.headline: Buba seen unwilling to use rates as mark booster.

text.p: Germany's central bank may be threatening to take action to help the ailing mark, but it is probably not prepared to use money market interest rates as a tool to jack up the currency, analysts say.

The Bundesbank has kept the markets guessing over the past two weeks over whether it will shift its policy on its regular securities repurchase, or repo, operations in order to allow the key repo rate to drift higher.

Such speculation was sparked late last month when, amid the dollar's prolonged rally against the mark, the Bundesbank set the repo rate for the first two weeks of its four-week summer break at a fixed 3.0 percent but not for the remaining two weekly tenders.

But the contrast between Germany's fragile economy and the health of its U.S. counterpart is so stark that Germany cannot yet afford to raise interest rates to levels where mark deposits attract the market to the same degree as dollars, analysts said.

"The real issue is not the technical one of whether they will switch and run a fixed and variable repo in tandem, but whether the German economy can withstand higher interest rates. And the answer is 'no'," said Stephen Yorke, deputy head of foreign exchange at SBC Warburg.
Germany's interest rates are among the lowest in the industrialised world. Only Japan and Switzerland have key rates that are lower than Germany's 3.00 percent discount rate.
Such fundamentals, and perceptions that European monetary union will replace the mark with a single currency that is less stable, have driven dollar/mark to its highest level in nearly eight years.
Dollar/mark bulls were given more encouragement on Wednesday by data showing German unemployment had increased slightly more than expected and was still at record-high levels.

"With German data showing unemployment stuck at very high levels, perceptions resurfaced that the German economic situation wasn't good and that under the circumstances, they just wouldn't be able to raise interest rates," said Masahiro Kawasaki, manager at Sakura Bank in London.
In such a dollar-bull environment, a technical tweak to raise money market rates was seen as a futile attempt.

"It's not going to change the main thrust of where this market wants to go and put dollar/mark into reverse...because the market is going to see through the technicalities to the substance," SBC's Yorke said.

Perceptions that the Bundesbank wanted to switch its money market policy faded further today when the central bank supplied the German money market with far more funds at its regular operations than anticipated .
Traders said this move showed the Bundesbank had passed up the opportunity to squeeze the market and push rates higher.

"If the Bundesbank had injected less funds than expected or withdrawn, it would have sparked speculation they might switch to a parallel repo at next week's tender," Sakura's Kawasaki said. "But that didn't happen, and dollar/mark shot up."
But analysts warned against jumping to conclusions on the basis of today's operations alone.
Mark Geddes, treasury economist at ABN AMRO, said the acid test was next week's repo, adding that there was a real prospect of higher rates if dollar/mark was above 1.90 next week.
But some analysts cautioned against overinterpreting today's money market operations.
"You can't read too much into it, because it's a highly technical measure that depends on the liquidity needs of the money market," said Ros Lifton, senior international economist at HSBC Markets.
"The Bundesbank rarely indicates its policies through adjustments in liquidity, it makes them quite clear in its rate options and what it says to the press," Lifton said.
And even if the Bundesbank does decide to conduct variable and fixed repos next week, analysts said, that move was unlikely to rein in dollar/mark for long.
"Maybe there won't even be a knee-jerk reaction. It's been so widely canvassed now, I think people will just shrug their shoulders," SBC's Yorke said.
